latin.2571: CXXXIV. Caeterum quanquam authores illius sententiae efficaciam gratiae velint esse aliquid in auxilio divino, quod voluntatis operationem antecedit; ac proinde quod ab ejus consensu & cooperatione ea ratione non pendet, ut in hominis potestate situm sit gratiam vel efficacem, vel inefficacem reddere, ut volunt Molina, & qui eum sequuntur: nihilominus non negant gratiae efficaciam a libero arbitrio aliquo modo pendere. Etenim, juxta ipsos, efficacia gratiae duobus modis considerari potest, vel in actu primo, vel in actu secundo. Priori modo spectata ea nihil aliud est, quam vis efficiendi, quae non distinguitur ab ipso auxilio: & hac ratione efficacia gratiae non pendet a libero arbitrio, sed a Deo. Posteriori modo efficacia gratiae sumitur pro ipsa efficientia, seu influxu actuali gratiae in opus supernaturale. Et sub hac etiam consideratione efficacia gratiae pendet a Deo. Sicut enim influxus instrumenti in opus pendet ab agente principali, quod tali instrumento utitur: ita influxus gratiae in opus supernaturale pendet a Deo, ut ab agente primario, quod per gratiam, ut per instrumentum quoddam suum, operatur. Verum quia haec actualis efficientia gratiae, non tantum pendet a Deo, sed etiam ab ipso libero arbitrio, ut a causa partiali, sine cujus operatione gratia non ageret, ideo dicunt hoc respectu, id est, in actu secundo, gratiae efficaciam etiam a libero arbitrio pendere. Quemadmodum ea de re mentem suam explicat Petrus a Sancto Joseph in tractatu de gratia divina disput. 7. num. 62.
latin.2572: CXXXV. Qualiscunque tamen sit illa dependentia gratiae efficacis, quoad actum secundum, a libero arbitrio; nihilominus ex eorum sensu, efficacia gratiae talis est, ut ea posita in actu primo, infallibiliter sequatur effectus, id est, liberi arbitrii consensus & cooperatio: siquidem auxilium illud efficax esse dicitur, quod efficaciter, & infallibiliter voluntatem movet ad consensum eliciendum, & facit ut faciat. Ut loquitur idem Petrus a Sancto Joseph in citata disputatione num. 61. Adeo ut supposita efficacia illa auxilii divini, quam habet a solo Deo, & antecedenter ad voluntatis consensum, nunquam contingere possit, ut homo non faciat illud ad quod ejusmodi auxilio movetur. Sicut ex adverso remota tali efficacia, quantumcunque gratia sufficiens supponatur, prorsus contingere nequit, ut sequatur illa bona operatio, ad quam sufficiens dicitur. Qua in re quoque a Molina discedunt, juxta cujus hypotheses, quacunque Dei gratia actualem voluntatis consensum antecedente posita, fieri potest ut effectus, ad quem ordinatur gratia, vel sequatur, vel non sequatur: nec in alterutram partem eventus infallibilis est.
latin.2573: CXXXVI. Neque tamen difficile putant istam eventus infallibilitatem, ad positionem, vel remotionem auxilii ejus quod efficax dicitur, cum humani arbitrii libertate conciliare. Quamvis enim nunquam eveniat, ut voluntas consensum suum deneget motionibus in quibus consistit gratia efficax, id est, quae secundum Dei praescientiam, ita voluntati congruunt, & sunt attemperatae, ut voluntatem flexurae sint; nihilominus voluntas motionibus illis praeventa & excitata, ab illis non praedeterminatur; sed seipsam ita ad agendum determinat, ut illis praesentibus possit non agere, & suspendere consensum, vel etiam ad dissensum se determinare, si natura ejusmodi motionum in se spectetur.
latin.2574: CXXXVII. Ac quamvis, ipsis fatentibus, quodammodo necesse sit, eum qui gratiam efficacem accepit, illi consentire, & ea praestare ad quae gratia illum movet; cum repugnet gratiam aliquam esse efficacem, & ea posita effectum non sequi: necessitas tamen illa libertati non officit; quoniam ex eorum doctrina, consequens est & non antecedens. Nam ipsis ea demum gratia efficax est, quae constat iis auxiliis, quae voluntati pro loco & tempore sic accommodata sunt, ut ab aeterno praeviderit Deus fore ut iis voluntas libere moveri se sinat, si ei offerantur, quanquam etiam resistere posset; adeoque in congruitate a qua gratia dicitur efficax, includitur libere futurus voluntatis consensus, a Deo per scientiam conditionatam ab aeterno praevisus. Ac proinde nullo modo libertatem hominis laedit, si dicamus necesse esse ut efficaci gratiae consentiat, cum ea solum gratia efficax appelletur, cui supponitur voluntas libere consensura, si Deus illam erga hominem adhibeat: & sic necessitas illa non praecedat, sed sequatur praevisum sub conditione voluntatis consensum.
latin.2575: CXXXVIII. Addunt gratiam efficacem in effectu suo producendo infallibilem esse, non absolute & Metaphysice, sed potius moraliter: quoniam cum sit voluntatis dispositioni maxime congrua & proportionata, voluntatem infallibiliter sed ratione admodum suavi, & voluntatis genio consentanea movet. Ad eum modum quo Homo summa egestate & inopia laborans, quamvis Physice possit centum aureos sibi oblatos respuere, tamen moraliter loquendo, positis rebus ut sunt, seu habita ratione status, conditionis, & calamitatis, eos infallibiliter acceptabit, quia sunt valde accommodati ad sublevandam illius miseriam.
latin.2576: CXXXIX. Denique gloriantur qui sunt in hac opinione, gratiae efficaciam sic a se expositam, non solum cum arbitrii humani libertate, optime consistere; sed etiam cum certitudine divinae praedestinationis. Quandoquidem secundum illam, praedestinatio habet suum effectum, per auxilia quidem in se repudiabilia; ita tamen genio voluntatis accommodata, ut juxta praescientiam Dei, effectum infallibiliter sint habitura.
latin.2577: CXL. Atque ita a nobis quam dilucide fieri potuit, breviter expositae sunt quatuor sententiae, in Schola Romana maxime solennes & receptae, circa gratiae divinae sufficientiam & efficaciam. Praeter quas etiam possent aliquot aliae referri: Sed quia videntur valde improbabiles, & authores obscuriores, ac sectatores pauciores habent; & prolixum nimis ac taediosum foret minutiora discrimina notare, quibus Doctores singuli aliquatenus inter se discrepant, his contenti esse possumus; nec videtur operae pretium in minutias istas scrupulosius inquirere.

sections.title: In what sense efficacy depends on free choice
sections.pass_a: CXXXIV. But although the authors of that opinion will have the efficacy of grace be something in the divine aid, which precedes the operation of the will; and therefore which does not depend on its consent & cooperation in such a way, that it is placed in man's power to render grace either efficacious, or inefficacious, as Molina will have it, & those who follow him: nevertheless they do not deny that the efficacy of grace depends in some way on free choice. For, according to them, the efficacy of grace can be considered in two ways, either in first act, or in second act. Regarded in the former way it is nothing else, than the power of effecting, which is not distinguished from the aid itself: & in this respect the efficacy of grace does not depend on free choice, but on God. In the latter way the efficacy of grace is taken for the very efficiency, or actual influence of grace on the supernatural work. And under this consideration also the efficacy of grace depends on God. For as the influence of an instrument on the work depends on the principal agent, which uses such an instrument: so the influence of grace on the supernatural work depends on God, as on the primary agent, who works through grace, as through a certain instrument of his own. But because this actual efficiency of grace, depends not only on God, but also on free choice itself, as on a partial cause, without whose operation grace would not act, therefore they say that in this respect, that is, in second act, the efficacy of grace depends also on free choice. As Peter of Saint Joseph explains his mind on this matter in the treatise on divine grace disput. 7. num. 62.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXIV. The authors of this view hold that the efficacy of grace is something in the divine aid that comes before the will's working, and so does not hang on the will's consent and cooperation in the way Molina and his followers claim, as though it lay in a person's power to make grace efficacious or inefficacious. Even so, they do not deny that the efficacy of grace depends on free choice in some way. On their account it can be considered in two ways, in first act or in second act. Taken the first way, it is simply the power to bring about the effect, which is not distinct from the aid itself; in this respect it depends not on free choice but on God.

Taken the second way, efficacy means the actual working itself, the actual influence of grace on the supernatural work; and in this respect too it depends on God. Just as an instrument's influence on a work depends on the principal agent using it, so the influence of grace on a supernatural work depends on God as primary agent, who works through grace as through an instrument of his own. Yet this actual working of grace depends not only on God but also on free choice itself, as a partial cause without whose operation grace would not act. In this respect, then, that is, in second act, they say the efficacy of grace also depends on free choice. So Peter of Saint Joseph explains his mind on the matter in the treatise on divine grace, disputation 7, number 62.

sections.title: Given efficacy in first act, consent follows infallibly
sections.pass_a: CXXXV. Whatever however be that dependence of efficacious grace, as to second act, on free choice; nevertheless in their sense, the efficacy of grace is such, that it being posited in first act, the effect follows infallibly, that is, the consent & cooperation of free choice: since that aid is said to be efficacious, which efficaciously, & infallibly moves the will to eliciting consent, & makes it act. As the same Peter of Saint Joseph speaks in the cited disputation num. 61. So that that efficacy of the divine aid being supposed, which it has from God alone, & antecedently to the consent of the will, it can never happen, that the man does not do that to which he is moved by such aid. As on the other hand such efficacy being removed, however much sufficient grace be supposed, it altogether cannot happen, that that good operation follows, for which it is called sufficient. In which matter also they depart from Molina, according to whose hypotheses, whatever grace of God preceding the actual consent of the will be posited, it can happen that the effect, to which the grace is ordered, either follows, or does not follow: nor is the outcome infallible in either direction.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXV. Whatever this dependence of efficacious grace on free choice in second act may be, on their view the efficacy of grace is such that, once it is in place in first act, the effect follows infallibly, namely the consent and cooperation of free choice. For an aid is called efficacious when it 'moves the will efficaciously and infallibly to give its consent, and makes it act', as the same Peter of Saint Joseph puts it in the disputation cited, number 61. Given that efficacy of the divine aid, which it has from God alone and prior to the will's consent, it can never happen that a person fails to do what such aid moves him to do.

Conversely, take that efficacy away, and however much sufficient grace is supposed, the good work for which it is called sufficient simply cannot follow. Here too they part from Molina. On his assumptions, whatever grace of God is given ahead of the will's actual consent, the effect it is directed to may follow or may not, and the outcome is infallible neither way.

sections.title: Infallibility reconciled with freedom
sections.pass_a: CXXXVI. Nor yet do they think it difficult to reconcile that infallibility of the outcome, upon the positing, or the removal of the aid which is called efficacious, with the freedom of human choice. For although it never happens, that the will denies its consent to the motions in which efficacious grace consists, that is, which according to the foreknowledge of God, so suit the will, & are attuned to it, that they will bend the will; nevertheless the will prevented & roused by those motions, is not predetermined by them; but determines itself to acting in such a way, that while they are present it can not act, & suspend consent, or even determine itself to dissent, if the nature of such motions be regarded in itself.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXVI. Nor do they find it hard to reconcile this infallibility of outcome, whether the aid called efficacious is given or withheld, with the freedom of human choice. It never happens, they say, that the will refuses consent to the motions that make up efficacious grace, that is, to motions which, according to God's foreknowledge, so suit the will and are so attuned to it that they will bend it.

Even so, the will, forestalled and stirred by those motions, is not predetermined by them. It determines itself to act in such a way that, while they are present, it could refrain from acting and withhold consent, or even settle on refusal, if the nature of such motions is considered in itself.

sections.title: A consequent necessity, from consent foreseen under condition
sections.pass_a: CXXXVII. And although, by their own admission, it is in a way necessary, that he who has received efficacious grace, consent to it, & perform those things to which grace moves him; since it is contradictory that some grace be efficacious, & the effect not follow when it is posited: yet that necessity does not hinder freedom; since by their doctrine, it is consequent & not antecedent. For to them that grace only is efficacious, which consists of those aids, which are so adjusted to the will for place & time, that God foresaw from eternity that the will would freely let itself be moved by them, if they were offered to it, although it could also resist; and so in the congruity from which grace is called efficacious, is included the consent of the will that will freely come about, foreseen by God from eternity through conditional knowledge. And therefore it in no way harms man's freedom, if we say that it is necessary that he consent to efficacious grace, since that grace only is called efficacious, to which the will is supposed as going to consent freely, if God apply it to the man: & so that necessity does not precede, but follows the consent of the will foreseen under condition.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXVII. They admit that in a way it is necessary for someone who has received efficacious grace to consent to it and do what it moves him to, since it is a contradiction for a grace to be efficacious and yet for the effect not to follow once it is given. But that necessity does not impair freedom, because on their teaching it is consequent, not antecedent.

For them, efficacious grace is precisely grace made up of aids so fitted to the will for the place and time that God foresaw from eternity that, if they were offered, the will would freely let itself be moved by them, though it could also resist. So the congruity that makes grace be called efficacious includes the will's future free consent, foreseen by God from eternity through conditional knowledge. Saying that a person must consent to efficacious grace therefore does no harm at all to his freedom. Only that grace is called efficacious to which the will is assumed to be about to consent freely if God applies it to the person; and so that necessity does not go before the will's consent, foreseen under a condition, but follows it.

sections.title: Moral, not metaphysical, infallibility
sections.pass_a: CXXXVIII. They add that efficacious grace is infallible in producing its effect, not absolutely & Metaphysically, but rather morally: since, as it is most congruous & proportioned to the disposition of the will, it moves the will infallibly but in a very gentle manner, & agreeable to the temper of the will. In the way in which a Man labouring under the utmost want & need, although Physically he can reject a hundred gold pieces offered to him, yet morally speaking, things being posited as they are, or account being had of his state, condition, & calamity, will infallibly accept them, because they are very well suited to relieving his misery.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXVIII. They add that efficacious grace is infallible in producing its effect not absolutely and metaphysically but rather morally. Being supremely congruous and proportioned to the will's disposition, it moves the will infallibly, yet in a very gentle way that agrees with the will's own temper.

It is like a man struggling with the direst want and poverty: physically he could turn down a hundred gold coins offered to him, but morally speaking, things being as they are, or given his state, situation and misfortune, he will infallibly accept them, because they are so well suited to relieving his distress.

sections.title: The claim to square with predestination too
sections.pass_a: CXXXIX. Finally those who are of this opinion boast that the efficacy of grace thus set forth by them, agrees excellently not only with the freedom of human choice; but also with the certainty of divine predestination. Since according to it, predestination has its effect, through aids indeed in themselves rejectable; yet so adjusted to the temper of the will, that according to the foreknowledge of God, they will infallibly have effect.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXIX. Lastly, those who hold this opinion pride themselves that the efficacy of grace, as they explain it, fits perfectly not only with the freedom of human choice but also with the certainty of divine predestination. On this view predestination achieves its effect through aids that can in themselves be rejected, yet are so suited to the will's temper that, in line with God's foreknowledge, they will take effect infallibly.

sections.title: Close of the four Roman opinions
sections.pass_a: CXL. And so by us as clearly as could be done, there have been briefly set forth the four opinions, most established & received in the Roman School, concerning the sufficiency & efficacy of divine grace. Besides which some others also could be reported: But because they seem very improbable, & have more obscure authors, and fewer followers; & it would be too prolix and tedious to note the finer differences, by which the several Doctors differ somewhat among themselves, we can be content with these; nor does it seem worth the trouble to inquire more scrupulously into those minutiae.
pass_b: Thesis CXL. So we have set out briefly, as clearly as we could, the four opinions on the sufficiency and efficacy of divine grace that are most established and accepted in the Roman School. Others could be reported as well. But they seem highly improbable, their authors are less known and their followers fewer, and it would be far too long and tedious to note the finer differences on which individual doctors partly disagree among themselves. We may rest content with these four, and it does not seem worth the effort to look more minutely into such details.
